claim: In Drosophila, graded expression of the maternal transcription factor Bicoid (Bcd) provides positional information to activate target genes at different positions along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: In Drosophila, graded expression of the maternal transcription factor Bicoid (Bcd) provides positional information to activate target genes at different positions along the anterior-posterior axis.
evidence: This is a well-established finding in the field, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The occupancy of target sequences by Bcd is not primarily determined by Bcd binding sites, but by chromatin context.
source: By measuring the biochemical affinity of target enhancers in these classes in vitro and genome-wide chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq, we found that the occupancy of target sequences by Bcd is not primarily determined by Bcd binding sites, but by chromatin context.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro affinity measurements and ATAC-seq experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bcd drives an open chromatin state at a subset of its targets.
source: Bcd drives an open chromatin state at a subset of its targets.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data showing reduced chromatin accessibility at certain Bcd targets in bcd mutants.

claim: Concentration-insensitive targets are found in more accessible chromatin and are bound at low concentrations.
source: Our data support a model where Bcd influences chromatin structure to gain access to concentration-sensitive targets at high concentrations, while concentration-insensitive targets are found in more accessible chromatin and are bound at low concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data showing differential binding and accessibility patterns across concentration classes.

claim: Bcd protein forms an anterior-to-posterior gradient in the embryo.
source: In early Drosophila melanogaster embryos, Bicoid (Bcd) protein forms an anterior-to-posterior gradient the embryo (Driever and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1988b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Driever and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1988b.

claim: Bcd functions as transcriptional activator to pattern the embryo, binding to target gene enhancers and activating gene expression at distinct positions along the AP axis, corresponding to different concentrations of Bcd protein.
source: Bcd functions as transcriptional activator to pattern the embryo, binding to target gene enhancers and activating gene expression at distinct positions along the AP axis, corresponding to different concentrations of Bcd protein (Driever and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1988a; Struhl et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Driever and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1988a and Struhl et al., 1989.

claim: Embryos in which the graded distribution of Bcd is disrupted still exhibit patterned expression of Bcd target genes.
source: Embryos in which the graded distribution of Bcd is disrupted still exhibit patterned expression of Bcd target genes, and these genes can be activated at lower concentrations of Bcd than these nuclei would be exposed to in a wild-type embryo (Chen et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013; Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013; Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2009.

claim: Bcd target genes can be activated at lower concentrations of Bcd than these nuclei would be exposed to in a wild-type embryo.
source: Embryos in which the graded distribution of Bcd is disrupted still exhibit patterned expression of Bcd target genes, and these genes can be activated at lower concentrations of Bcd than these nuclei would be exposed to in a wild-type embryo (Chen et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013; Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2013; Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2009.

claim: The posterior boundaries of Bcd target genes are positioned by a system of repressors including Runt, Krüppel, and Capicua.
source: Chen et al. have shown that the posterior boundaries of Bcd target genes are positioned by a system of repressors including Runt, Krüppel, and Capicua.
evidence: This is attributed to work by Chen et al., implying citation support.

claim: Bcd is able to bind cooperatively to achieve sharp concentration thresholds.
source: Direct measurements of Bcd binding affinity have been conducted in vitro using DNA probes (Burz et al., 1998; Gao and Finkelstein, 1998; Yuan et al., 1996; Ma et al., 1996) and have demonstrated that Bcd is able to bind cooperatively to achieve sharp concentration thresholds.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Burz et al., 1998; Gao and Finkelstein, 1998; Yuan et al., 1996; Ma et al., 1996.

claim: Little correlation has been shown between predicted binding site affinity and AP position of gene expression.
source: While these measurements lend some support to a simple affinity model, little correlation has been shown between predicted binding site affinity and AP position of gene expression (Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2005; Segal et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2005 and Segal et al., 2008.

claim: A list of 1027 robust and reproducible Bcd binding regions was established.
source: We performed the ChIP-seq experiments on embryos expressing GFP-tagged Bcd in a bcd null mutant background that were staged precisely in nuclear cycle 14 (NC14), and established a list of robust and reproducible list of 1027 peak Bcd binding regions (see Supplementary file 1 and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ChIP-seq peaks successfully identify 63 of the 66 previously characterized Bcd target enhancers.
source: These peaks successfully identify 63 of the 66 previously characterized Bcd target enhancers shown to drive expression patterns that span broadly across the AP axis (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of ChIP-seq data with previously characterized enhancers from Chen et al., 2012.

claim: The gap genes buttonhead (btd) and knirps (kni) have anterior expression domains that are not present in bcd mutant embryos.
source: For example, the gap genes buttonhead (btd) and knirps (kni) have anterior expression domains that are not present in bcd mutant embryos (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The posterior kni expression domain is expressed in bcd embryos, albeit with shifted positional boundaries.
source: The posterior kni expression domain, however, is expressed in bcd embryos, albeit with shifted positional boundaries.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The distinct domains of kni expression are controlled by separate enhancer elements.
source: These distinct domains of kni expression are controlled by separate enhancer elements (Pankratz et al., 1992; Schroeder et al., 2004), both of which are bound by Bcd in vivo (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pankratz et al., 1992 and Schroeder et al., 2004, and by ChIP-seq data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Both kni enhancers are bound by Bcd in vivo.
source: These distinct domains of kni expression are controlled by separate enhancer elements (Pankratz et al., 1992; Schroeder et al., 2004), both of which are bound by Bcd in vivo (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: In bcd nos hb tsl quadruple mutants, kni expression is reduced to near-background levels.
source: In the absence of all maternal AP patterning inputs (bicoid nanos hunchback torsolike [bcd nos hb tsl] quadruple mutants), kni expression is reduced to near-background levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and is not expressed in a posterior stripe.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In nos hb tsl triple mutants, the kni posterior expression domain has a near wild-type level and anterior boundary.
source: However, in embryos where Bcd is the sole source of maternal patterning information (nos hb tsl triple mutants), the kni posterior expression domain has a near wild-type level and anterior boundary (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Loss of the posterior and terminal systems (nos and tsl) does not alter the Bcd ChIP-seq profile.
source: We used the statistical package EdgeR (Robinson et al., 2010) to test for differential Bcd binding between wild-type and nos tsl embryos and found that we could not detect any significant change in binding at any of these 1027 regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analyzed with EdgeR and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The physical interaction of Bcd with DNA occurs independently of other maternal AP patterning inputs.
source: Therefore, although the expression domains of Bcd target genes are ultimately influenced by inputs from other AP patterning systems, the physical interaction of Bcd with DNA occurs independently of other maternal AP patterning inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing no change in Bcd binding in nos tsl mutants.

claim: The endogenous bcd promoter drives a level of uniformly expressed Bcd equivalent to that measured at approximately 65% egg length of the wild-type gradient.
source: The endogenous bcd promoter drives a level of uniformly expressed Bcd equivalent to that measured at approximately 65% egg length of the wild-type gradient.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The matrimony (mtrm) and αTubulin67C (αTub67C) promoters drive expression levels corresponding to approximately 45% and 25% egg length, respectively.
source: The matrimony (mtrm) and αTubulin67C (αTub67C) promoters drive expression levels corresponding to approximately 45% and 25% egg length, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Uniform expression of Bcd confers gene expression profiles and developmental programs representative of distinct positions along the AP axis.
source: Uniform expression of Bcd confers gene expression profiles and developmental programs representative of distinct positions along the AP axis.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and cuticle preparation data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: The head gap gene buttonhead (btd) expands to fill the entire middle of the embryo at the highest level of uniform Bcd.
source: The head gap gene buttonhead (btd) is expressed in an anterior stripe in wild-type embryos (Figure 1A), but expands to fill the entire middle of the embryo at the highest level of uniform Bcd (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At the medium level of uniform Bcd, the Btd anterior stripe is duplicated at the posterior.
source: At the medium level, the Btd anterior stripe is duplicated at the posterior, and at the lowest Bcd level, it is not expressed.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At the lowest Bcd level, Btd is not expressed.
source: At the medium level, the Btd anterior stripe is duplicated at the posterior, and at the lowest Bcd level, it is not expressed.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The gap gene knirps shows a duplication of its anterior domain in the posterior in high uniform Bcd embryos.
source: The gap gene knirps, which is expressed in an anterior domain and a posterior stripe, shows a duplication of its anterior domain in the posterior in high uniform Bcd embryos.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is a weaker duplication of the kni anterior domain at the medium Bcd level.
source: There is also a weaker duplication at the medium Bcd level.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is no apparent anterior kni expression at the lowest Bcd level, but an expanded posterior stripe is present.
source: There is no apparent anterior expression at the lowest level, but an expanded posterior stripe is present.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The uniform Bcd transgenes can specify cell fates that reflect their relative expression levels.
source: These effects on the body plan indicate that the uniform Bcd transgenes can specify cell fates that reflect their relative expression levels.
evidence: This is supported by cuticle preparation data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Four different classes of Bcd binding peaks were identified: one concentration-insensitive class, and three classes with increasing sensitivity to Bcd concentration.
source: Using EdgeR (Robinson et al., 2010), we selected peak regions that exhibited statistically significant (FDR ≤ 0.05) differences in binding by performing pairwise exact tests between the three uniform Bcd concentrations. This yielded four different classes of peaks, one concentration-insensitive class, and three classes with increasing sensitivity to Bcd concentration.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analyzed with EdgeR and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Concentration-Insensitive peaks (n = 143) show no significant differences between any of the concentrations of uniform Bcd tested.
source: The Concentration-Insensitive peak class (n = 143) shows no significant differences between any of the concentrations of uniform Bcd we tested.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analyzed with EdgeR and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Concentration-Sensitive III peaks (n = 593) are significantly reduced in binding between the highest and lowest Bcd concentrations, but reductions are not significant between high and medium, or medium and low.
source: Concentration-Sensitive III peaks (n = 593) are significantly reduced in binding between the highest and lowest Bcd concentrations, but reductions are not significant between high and medium, or medium and low.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analyzed with EdgeR and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Concentration-Sensitive II peaks (n = 138) are significantly reduced in binding at the lowest Bcd level compared to either the medium or the high levels.
source: Concentration-Sensitive II peaks (n = 138) are significantly reduced in binding at the lowest Bcd level compared to either the medium or the high levels.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analyzed with EdgeR and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Concentration-Sensitive I peaks (n = 152) are significantly reduced in binding at both the medium and the low Bcd levels compared to the highest level.
source: Finally, Concentration-Sensitive I peaks (n = 152) are significantly reduced in binding at both the medium and the low Bcd levels compared to the highest level (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data analyzed with EdgeR and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Bcd binds differentially to its targets at specific concentrations.
source: These different groups suggest that Bcd binds differentially to its targets at specific concentrations, and furthermore that certain subsets of these targets are bound only in anterior nuclei whereas others are bound broadly across the entire AP axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing different concentration sensitivity classes.

claim: Certain subsets of Bcd targets are bound only in anterior nuclei whereas others are bound broadly across the entire AP axis.
source: These different groups suggest that Bcd binds differentially to its targets at specific concentrations, and furthermore that certain subsets of these targets are bound only in anterior nuclei whereas others are bound broadly across the entire AP axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing different concentration sensitivity classes.

claim: Within the set of known Bcd targets, there is strong correlation between position of expression and the associated Bcd sensitivity class.
source: Within the set of known Bcd targets, there is strong correlation between position of expression and the associated Bcd sensitivity class (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of ChIP-seq sensitivity classes with known enhancer expression patterns shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A total of 293 Vienna Tiles overlap with at least one peak in the Bcd ChIP-seq data set.
source: A total of 293 Tiles overlap with at least one peak in our data set.
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis between Vienna Tile enhancers and ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: 163 Vienna Tiles drive gene expression in stage 4–6 and overlap with a total of 151 (14.7%) of the Bcd-peaks.
source: Of these, 163 drive gene expression in stage 4–6 (which includes NC14), and these active Tiles overlap with a total of 151 (14.7%) of the Bcd-peaks (Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis between Vienna Tile enhancers and ChIP-seq peaks shown in Table 2.

claim: The fraction of Vienna Tiles that overlap with Bcd peaks and are active during early development (55.6%) is significantly higher than the proportion of Tiles active in early embryos for the collection as a whole (8.5%).
source: The fraction of the 293 Tiles that overlap with Bcd peaks and are active during early development (163, or 55.6%) is significantly higher than the proportion of Tiles active in early embryos for the collection as a whole (666 of the total 7793 or 8.5%).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of overlap frequencies.

claim: The Bcd binding peaks are significantly enriched for enhancer activity.
source: This suggests that the Bcd binding peaks are significantly enriched for enhancer activity, and that a similar fraction of the remaining 793 Bcd peaks not present in the Fly Enhancer collection may correspond to active enhancers as well.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of active Vienna Tiles in Bcd ChIP peaks.

claim: The Concentration-Sensitive III peaks have the lowest representation in the Fly Enhancer collection, with 18% of peaks overlapping with a Vienna Tile enhancer reporter.
source: While the Concentration-Sensitive III peaks are the largest class, they have the lowest representation in the Fly Enhancer collection, with 18% of peaks overlapping with a Vienna Tile enhancer reporter.
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: Of the Concentration-Sensitive III peaks overlapping with Vienna Tiles, 52% overlap with Tiles active at stage 4–6, a smaller fraction than observed for the other peak classes which range from 73% to 77%.
source: Of these overlapping peaks, 52% overlap with Tiles active at stage 4–6, a smaller fraction than observed for the other peak classes which range from 73% to 77% (see Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: The Concentration Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes are nearly twice as likely to lie within 500 bp of a TSS.
source: We also observe differences in the proximity of peaks in each class to transcription start sites (TSS), with the Concentration Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes being nearly twice as likely to lie within 500 bp of a TSS (see Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by proximity analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: The Bcd sensitivity classes are predictive of the expression domains of associated enhancer fragments.
source: The Bcd sensitivity classes are predictive of the expression domains of associated enhancer fragments. Enhancers overlapping with both the Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes drive expression in anterior regions of the embryo, with the Concentration-Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes driving broad and posterior expression, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Vienna Tile expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Enhancers overlapping with the Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes drive expression in anterior regions of the embryo.
source: Enhancers overlapping with both the Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes drive expression in anterior regions of the embryo, with the Concentration-Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes driving broad and posterior expression, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Vienna Tile expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Concentration-Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes drive broad and posterior expression, respectively.
source: Enhancers overlapping with both the Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes drive expression in anterior regions of the embryo, with the Concentration-Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes driving broad and posterior expression, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Vienna Tile expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The top three most highly ranked motifs in Bcd ChIP peaks were the consensus binding site for Zelda (Zld), and a strong (TAATCC) and weak (TAAGCC) Bcd binding site.
source: We identified the top motifs in the entire Bcd ChIP peak list, ranked by their e-value, and found that the top three most highly ranked motifs were the consensus binding site for the proposed pioneer factor Zelda (Zld) (ten Bosch et al., 2006; De Renzis et al., 2007; Harrison et al., 2011; Nien et al., 2011), and a strong (TAATCC) and weak (TAAGCC) Bcd binding site (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by de novo motif discovery using RSAT shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes are enriched for both the strong and weak Bcd sites relative to the peak set as a whole.
source: We found that despite their failure to bind Bcd at low concentrations, the Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes are enriched for both the strong and weak Bcd sites relative to the peak set as a whole.
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The Concentration-Sensitive III class did not contain an enrichment of any site over the total peak set.
source: The Concentration-Sensitive III class did not contain an enrichment of any site over the total peak set.
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The Concentration-Insensitive class showed a higher prevalence of the Zld binding site relative to the total peak set than any other class.
source: The Concentration-Insensitive class, however, showed a higher prevalence of the Zld binding site relative to the total peak set than any other class.
evidence: This is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is a correlation between the binding site number and position of gene expression.
source: Given our result that the Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes drive expression primarily in the anterior of the embryo (Figure 2B), the higher density of Bcd binding sites in these peaks indicates that there is, in fact, a correlation between the binding site number and position of gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of motif enrichment and expression pattern data.

claim: Bcd targets that behave as concentration-sensitive and -insensitive in vivo are not distinguished by their representation of strong versus weak Bcd binding sites.
source: However, in contrast to a binding site affinity model for Bcd function, Bcd targets that behave as concentration-sensitive and -insensitive in vivo are not distinguished by their representation of strong versus weak Bcd binding sites, partially confirming the previous study (Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from the motif enrichment analysis and supported by citation to Ochoa-Espinosa et al., 2005.

claim: Little correlation was found between in vitro binding affinity by EMSA and the in vivo binding properties observed by ChIP for a selected subset of peaks.
source: In further support of this concept, we found little correlation between in vitro binding affinity by electrophoretic mobility shift assay and the in vivo binding properties we observe by ChIP for a selected subset of peaks (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a bias toward both Bcd sites in peaks that show concentration-sensitive binding properties by ChIP-seq and a bias toward Zld sites in the concentration-insensitive peaks.
source: At the level of sequence composition, they instead appear to differ in their balance of Bcd and Zld binding sites. Although both strong and weak Bcd sites and Zld sites are enriched in the Bcd ChIP peaks as a whole, there is a bias toward both Bcd sites in peaks that show concentration-sensitive binding properties by ChIP-seq and a bias toward Zld sites in the concentration-insensitive peaks.
evidence: This is inferred from the motif enrichment analysis.

claim: Zld has been implicated in chromatin remodeling prior to zygotic genome activation.
source: Zld, a ubiquitously expressed early embryonic transcription factor, has been implicated in chromatin remodeling prior to zygotic genome activation (Harrison et al., 2011; Nien et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harrison et al., 2011; Nien et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2015.

claim: The chromatin context of an enhancer may play a greater role in its overall affinity for a transcription factor in vivo than the sequences of the binding sites that it contains.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the chromatin context of an enhancer may play a greater role in its overall affinity for a transcription factor in vivo than the sequences of the binding sites that it contains.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined motif and chromatin accessibility data.

claim: 13,266 peaks of chromatin accessibility were identified by ATAC-seq.
source: To measure genome-wide patterns of chromatin accessibility and nucleosome positioning, we performed ATAC-seq (Buenrostro et al., 2015) on single wild-type embryos precisely staged at 12 min after the onset of NC14, and identified 13,266 peaks of chromatin accessibility (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data.

claim: 855 (83.3%) of the 1,027 Bcd-bound regions overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
source: Of the 1,027 Bcd-bound regions identified by ChIP-seq, 855 (83.3%) of them overlap with ATAC-seq peaks.
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis between ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data.

claim: Of the total 13,226 accessible regions at NC14, 2675 (20.2%) show a significant reduction in accessibility in zld mutant embryos.
source: Of the total 13,226 accessible regions at NC14, 2675 (20.2%) show a significant reduction in accessibility in zld mutant embryos.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data in zld mutants analyzed with EdgeR.

claim: 402 (39.1%) of the 1,027 Bcd-bound peaks show reduced accessibility in zld mutants.
source: This fraction is higher in Bcd-bound peaks; 402 (39.1%; or 379 [44.3%] of the 855 Bcd peaks that overlap with ATAC open regions, see Table 5) show reduced accessibility in zld mutants, indicating that Bcd bound regions are more likely to be dependent on Zld for their accessibility than the genome as a whole.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data in zld mutants analyzed with EdgeR.

claim: Bcd bound regions are more likely to be dependent on Zld for their accessibility than the genome as a whole.
source: This fraction is higher in Bcd-bound peaks; 402 (39.1%; or 379 [44.3%] of the 855 Bcd peaks that overlap with ATAC open regions, see Table 5) show reduced accessibility in zld mutants, indicating that Bcd bound regions are more likely to be dependent on Zld for their accessibility than the genome as a whole.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Zld-dependent accessibility in Bcd peaks versus genome-wide.

claim: The Zld-dependent peaks are distributed across each sensitivity class determined by ChIP, with no particular class being significantly more Zld-dependent.
source: However, the Zld-dependent peaks are distributed across each sensitivity class determined by ChIP, with no particular class being significantly more Zld-dependent (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: If the Bcd peaks are separated into those bound and not bound by Zld, an enrichment of the Concentration-Insensitive peaks is observed in Zld-dependent, Zld-bound peaks.
source: However, if the Bcd peaks are separated into those bound and not bound by Zld, we do observe an enrichment of the Concentration-Insensitive peaks in Zld-dependent, Zld-bound peaks (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zld contributes to the accessibility of a subset of Bcd targets, but is unlikely to be the sole determinant of the differential concentration sensitivity of Bcd peaks as a whole.
source: These results suggest that while Zld contributes to the accessibility of a subset of Bcd targets, it is unlikely to be the sole determinant of the differential concentration sensitivity of Bcd peaks as a whole.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATAC-seq and enrichment analysis data.

claim: In bcd mutants, 326 (2.4%) of the 13,266 open regions in wild-type embryos show significantly reduced accessibility accompanied by increased nucleosome occupancy.
source: In bcd mutants, 326 (2.4%) of the 13,266 open regions in wild-type embryos show significantly reduced accessibility accompanied by increased nucleosome occupancy in those same regions (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data in bcd mutants shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: 132 (12.9%) of the 1,027 Bcd ChIP-seq peaks show reduced accessibility in the absence of Bcd and likely represent regions where Bcd's impact is direct.
source: More strikingly, 132 (12.9%) of the 1,027 Bcd ChIP-seq peaks show reduced accessibility in the absence of Bcd and likely represent regions where Bcd's impact is direct.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data in bcd mutants.

claim: Regions dependent on Bcd for accessibility are significantly enriched for peaks in the Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes.
source: These regions dependent on Bcd for accessibility are significantly enriched for peaks in the Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes (32.9% and 31.9% of each class, with Fisher's exact test P-values of 4.29 × 10−12 and 1.37 × 10−10, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis using Fisher's exact test shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Concentration-Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes are both significantly underrepresented in Bcd-dependent peaks.
source: In contrast, the Concentration-Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes are both significantly underrepresented (6.07% and 0.7% and p-values=7.88×10−13 and 2.29 × 10−8) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis using Fisher's exact test shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Bcd binding influences chromatin accessibility preferentially at a subset of highly concentration-sensitive targets.
source: This suggests that Bcd binding influences chromatin accessibility preferentially at a subset of highly concentration-sensitive targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of Bcd-dependent accessibility in Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes.

claim: Bcd's effects on chromatin accessibility at concentration-sensitive targets likely occurs only in anterior regions of the embryo.
source: Because the Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes are bound primarily at high Bcd concentrations, Bcd's effects on chromatin accessibility at these targets likely occurs only in anterior regions of the embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from the concentration-dependent binding and accessibility data.

claim: Chromatin accessibility at Bcd-dependent, concentration-sensitive targets is responsive to Bcd concentration.
source: In support of this, we find that chromatin accessibility at Bcd-dependent, concentration-sensitive targets is responsive to Bcd concentration. Expressing uniform Bcd confers accessibility to peaks that are not accessible in bcd mutant embryos (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data in uniform Bcd embryos shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The degree of chromatin accessibility conferred by Bcd correlates positively with the concentration of uniform Bcd expressed.
source: The degree of chromatin accessibility conferred by Bcd correlates positively with the concentration of uniform Bcd expressed (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data in uniform Bcd embryos shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Bcd influences the chromatin state of concentration-sensitive targets primarily at the high concentrations found in the anterior of the embryo.
source: This observation, along with the overrepresentation of the Concentration-Sensitive I and II classes in the Bcd-dependent peaks, suggests that Bcd influences the chromatin state of these targets primarily at the high concentrations found in the anterior of the embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from the concentration-dependent accessibility and enrichment data.

claim: Bcd bound regions in wild-type embryos are generally depleted of nucleosomes.
source: Bcd bound regions in wild-type embryos are generally depleted of nucleosomes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by nucleosome occupancy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The Concentration-Sensitive I and II Bcd peak classes are more likely to bind nucleosomes than the Concentration-Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes.
source: However, predicting nucleosome positioning sequences using the NuPoP algorithm (Xi et al., 2010) suggests that the Concentration-Sensitive I and II Bcd peak classes are more likely to bind nucleosomes than the Concentration-Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes. (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by predicted nucleosome occupancy data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The contrast between predicted nucleosome occupancy and observed depletion suggests that Bcd-bound regions are actively restructured for Bcd and other transcription factors to bind.
source: The contrast between predicted occupancy and observed depletion suggests that these regions are actively restructured for Bcd and other transcription factors to bind.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of predicted and observed nucleosome occupancy.

claim: Bcd, either directly or in combination with cofactors, is able to direct chromatin remodeling events.
source: The increased nucleosome preference of the more Concentration-Sensitive peaks, combined with the observation that these sites become occupied by nucleosomes in bcd mutants suggests a model where Bcd, either directly or in combination with cofactors is able to direct chromatin remodeling events, which may play a significant role in distinguishing concentration-sensitive and -insensitive targets.
evidence: This is inferred from the nucleosome occupancy and accessibility data.

claim: Bcd-bound regions that are dependent on either Zld or Bcd for their accessibility are more likely to have a higher nucleosome preference than regions that are independent of both factors.
source: Additionally, we find that Bcd-bound regions that are dependent on either Zld or Bcd for their accessibility are more likely to have a higher nucleosome preference than regions that are independent of both factors (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by predicted nucleosome occupancy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Bcd is able to overcome a high nucleosome barrier in a manner similar to Zld at a subset of its target enhancers.
source: This further suggests that Bcd is able to overcome a high nucleosome barrier in a manner similar to Zld (Sun et al., 2015) at a subset of its target enhancers.
evidence: This is inferred from the nucleosome preference data and supported by citation to Sun et al., 2015.

claim: In wild-type embryos, there is a gradual increase in average motif accessibility from high to low sensitivity.
source: In wild-type embryos, there is a gradual increase in average motif accessibility from high to low sensitivity, and this difference becomes more pronounced in bcd mutant embryos (Figure 4D), consistent with a role for Bcd in driving changes in accessibility at more sensitive sites in a concentration dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by motif accessibility analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The difference in motif accessibility becomes more pronounced in bcd mutant embryos.
source: In wild-type embryos, there is a gradual increase in average motif accessibility from high to low sensitivity, and this difference becomes more pronounced in bcd mutant embryos (Figure 4D), consistent with a role for Bcd in driving changes in accessibility at more sensitive sites in a concentration dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by motif accessibility analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: On average across all sensitivity classes, 55 ± 2% of Bcd motifs are in nucleosome-free tracts in wild-type embryos.
source: Calculating the fraction of motifs that overlap nucleosomes in either wild-type or bcd mutant chromatin conformations, we find that whereas on average across all sensitivity classes 55 ± 2% of Bcd motifs are in nucleosome-free tracts in wild-type embryos, in bcd mutant embryos motifs have lower overall accessibility and a graded association with nucleosomes that correlates with the sensitivity classes (41%, 46%, 50%, and 53% of motifs are accessible from high to low sensitivity).
evidence: This is supported by nucleosome-motif overlap analysis.

claim: In bcd mutant embryos, motifs have lower overall accessibility and a graded association with nucleosomes that correlates with the sensitivity classes.
source: Calculating the fraction of motifs that overlap nucleosomes in either wild-type or bcd mutant chromatin conformations, we find that whereas on average across all sensitivity classes 55 ± 2% of Bcd motifs are in nucleosome-free tracts in wild-type embryos, in bcd mutant embryos motifs have lower overall accessibility and a graded association with nucleosomes that correlates with the sensitivity classes (41%, 46%, 50%, and 53% of motifs are accessible from high to low sensitivity).
evidence: This is supported by nucleosome-motif overlap analysis.

claim: The mechanistic determinants of concentration-dependent Bcd action likely involve a complex interaction between Bcd, DNA, and chromatin structure.
source: These results indicate that the mechanistic determinants of concentration-dependent Bcd action likely involve a complex interaction between Bcd, DNA, and chromatin structure.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined motif accessibility and nucleosome occupancy data.

claim: The truncated Bcd protein (GFP-Bcd085) forms a gradient from the anterior of the embryo and is expressed at a similar level as a full-length GFP-Bcd.
source: The truncated protein (known as GFP-Bcd085) forms a gradient from the anterior of the embryo, and is expressed at a similar level as a full-length GFP-Bcd (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GFP-Bcd085 binding in the Concentration-Sensitive I and II peak classes was significantly reduced compared to wild-type.
source: By ChIP-seq, we found that GFP-Bcd085 binding in the Concentration-Sensitive I and II peak classes was significantly reduced compared to wild-type (p-values<0.0001 in permutation test with n = 10,000 trials), while binding to the Concentration-Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes was not (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: GFP-Bcd085 binding to the Concentration-Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes was not significantly reduced compared to wild-type.
source: By ChIP-seq, we found that GFP-Bcd085 binding in the Concentration-Sensitive I and II peak classes was significantly reduced compared to wild-type (p-values<0.0001 in permutation test with n = 10,000 trials), while binding to the Concentration-Sensitive III and Concentration-Insensitive classes was not (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Bcd's ability to access its concentration-sensitive targets is dependent upon activities carried out by domains in the C-terminus of the protein, likely via recruitment of a cofactor.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Bcd's ability to access its concentration-sensitive targets is dependent upon activities carried out by domains in the C-terminus of the protein, likely via recruitment of a cofactor, and that its DNA binding activity alone is insufficient to drive chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is inferred from the truncated Bcd ChIP-seq data.

claim: Bcd's DNA binding activity alone is insufficient to drive chromatin accessibility.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Bcd's ability to access its concentration-sensitive targets is dependent upon activities carried out by domains in the C-terminus of the protein, likely via recruitment of a cofactor, and that its DNA binding activity alone is insufficient to drive chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is inferred from the truncated Bcd ChIP-seq data.

claim: An enhancer for caudal is a Concentration-Insensitive Bcd target and drives expression in the posterior of the embryo.
source: Overall, highly concentration-dependent targets are expressed in the anterior and are dependent on Bcd for accessibility, while less sensitive targets show more posterior expression patterns and a greater enrichment for Zld binding sites. An enhancer for caudal is a Concentration-Insensitive Bcd target and drives expression in the posterior of the embryo (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The caudal enhancer depends on Zld for chromatin accessibility and is not functional in zld mutants.
source: This enhancer depends on Zld for chromatin accessibility, and consequently is not functional in zld mutants (Supplementary file 1 and Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data in Supplementary file 1 and reporter expression data in Figure 6B.

claim: The caudal enhancer is Bcd independent for chromatin accessibility and its expression boundary shifts anteriorly in bcd mutant embryos.
source: Like the kni posterior enhancer (Figure 1A), the caudal enhancer is Bcd independent for chromatin accessibility and its expression boundary shifts anteriorly in bcd mutant embryos.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq and reporter expression data.

claim: Mutating Zld binding sites to Bcd binding sites in the caudal enhancer results in a shift of caudal reporter expression to the anterior of the embryo.
source: We identified the Zld binding sites in the caudal enhancer sequence and mutated them to Bcd binding sites (Figure 6A). These mutations result in a shift of caudal reporter expression to the anterior of the embryo.
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Anterior expression of the mutated caudal reporter is Bcd dependent, as it is lost in bcd mutant embryos.
source: Anterior expression of the mutated reporter is Bcd dependent, as it is lost in bcd mutant embryos.
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The mutant caudal enhancer is functional in zld mutant embryos, retaining a distinct anterior expression domain.
source: Importantly, the mutant enhancer is functional in zld mutant embryos, retaining a distinct anterior expression domain.
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the absence of Zld binding, the wild-type caudal enhancer does not drive expression.
source: In the absence of Zld binding, the wild-type enhancer does not drive expression (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: By replacing Zld motifs with Bcd motifs, the caudal enhancer retains functionality, but the spatial domains of expression are now restricted to regions of high Bcd concentration.
source: By replacing Zld motifs with Bcd motifs, the enhancer retains functionality, but the spatial domains of expression are now restricted to regions of high Bcd concentration.
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Adding Bcd sites instead of Zld sites to the HC_45 reporter activates expression from the enhancer in an anterior stripe.
source: We found that adding Bcd sites instead of Zld sites to this same reporter also activates expression from the enhancer in an anterior stripe (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Bcd delineates distinct gene expression and chromatin states at specific positions along its concentration gradient.
source: These data support a model where Bcd delineates distinct gene expression and chromatin states at specific positions along its concentration gradient.
evidence: This is inferred from the reporter expression and chromatin accessibility data.

claim: The positional information in the Bcd gradient is read out as differential binding between Bcd and the cis-regulatory regions of its target genes.
source: The results presented here demonstrate that the positional information in the Bcd gradient is read out as differential binding between Bcd and the cis-regulatory regions of its target genes.
evidence: This is supported by the ChIP-seq data showing concentration-dependent binding.

claim: The differences in binding affinities observed in vivo cannot be explained entirely by the sequence of Bcd binding sites in the target enhancers.
source: However, motif analysis and in vitro EMSA experiments reveal that the differences in binding affinities that we observe in vivo cannot be explained entirely by the sequence of Bcd binding sites in the target enhancers.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis and EMSA data.

claim: A subset of the enhancers in the concentration-sensitive classes require Bcd for chromatin accessibility.
source: Instead we find that a subset of the enhancers in the concentration-sensitive classes require Bcd for chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data in bcd mutants.

claim: The Bcd morphogen establishes concentration thresholds along the AP axis by driving opening chromatin states at high concentrations.
source: Taken together, this leads us to model in which the Bcd morphogen establishes concentration thresholds along the AP axis of the developing embryo by driving opening chromatin states at high concentrations, thereby gaining access to its most sensitive target enhancers.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the combined ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data.

claim: At lower concentrations in more posterior nuclei, Bcd is unable to access concentration-sensitive enhancers, and therefore does not bind and activate their transcription.
source: At lower concentrations in more posterior nuclei, Bcd is unable to access these enhancers, and therefore does not bind and activate their transcription (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a model inferred from the combined ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Expression of concentration-sensitive target genes is restricted to anterior regions of the embryo.
source: In this way, expression of these concentration-sensitive target genes is restricted to anterior regions of the embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from the model and supported by expression data.

claim: The higher density of Bcd binding sites in highly concentration-sensitive target enhancers suggests that these targets may require a larger number of Bcd molecules to be bound at a given time to keep them free of nucleosomes and accessible.
source: The higher density of Bcd binding sites in highly concentration-sensitive target enhancers (shown in Figure 2D) suggests that these targets may require a larger number of Bcd molecules to be bound at a given time to keep them free of nucleosomes and accessible to the additional regulatory factors.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the motif enrichment data.

claim: The concentration thresholds in the Bcd gradient are read out molecularly at the level of chromatin accessibility, rather than through the strength of binding sites in the target sequences.
source: We therefore provide a model for morphogen function in which the concentration thresholds in the gradient are read out molecularly at the level of chromatin accessibility, rather than through the strength of binding sites in the target sequences.
evidence: This is a model inferred from the combined data.

claim: Bcd establishes initial patterns by interacting with default nucleosome positions in the early embryo, not by competing with its own target genes.
source: In our model Bcd establishes these initial patterns not by competing with its own target genes, but with default nucleosome positions in the early embryo.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the model.

claim: The initial interaction of Bcd with chromatin is an essential event for establishing distinct, positionally defined patterns of gene expression.
source: We predict that this initial interaction with chromatin is an essential event for establishing distinct, positionally defined patterns of gene expression.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the model.

claim: The chromatin landscapes established early by Bcd are elaborated upon by additional patterning factors, including Bcd target genes themselves, as well as repressor gradients.
source: The chromatin landscapes established early by Bcd are then elaborated upon by additional patterning factors, including Bcd target genes themselves, as well as the repressor gradients proposed by Chen, et al. (Chen et al., 2012)
evidence: This is inferred from the model and supported by citation to Chen et al., 2012.

claim: The pre-transcriptional information presented by Bcd in the form of differential binding states is refined at the level of gene expression domains by Bcd and other transcription factors active in the early embryo.
source: Thus, the pre-transcriptional information presented by Bcd in the form of differential binding states is refined at the level of gene expression domains both by Bcd and other transcription factors active in the early embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from the model.

claim: Zld contributes to the accessibility of Bcd targets in the genome, in part at those targets that are not dependent on Bcd for their accessibility.
source: The prominence of the Zld binding motif in the Bcd-bound ChIP peaks and ATAC-seq in zld mutants reveals that Zld also contributes to the accessibility of Bcd targets in the genome, in part at those targets that are not dependent on Bcd for their accessibility (61/1,027 peaks are dependent on both Bcd and Zld for accessibility).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data in zld mutants.

claim: Zld is likely one component that influences the accessibility and therefore the apparent in vivo affinity of the peaks that are bound by Bcd but insensitive to its local concentration.
source: Zld is therefore likely to be one component that influences the accessibility and therefore the apparent in vivo affinity of the peaks that are bound by Bcd but insensitive to its local concentration (Figure 7).
evidence: This is inferred from the ATAC-seq and motif data.

claim: Zld can extend the effective range of the dorsal-ventral morphogen Dorsal and aid in establishing concentration thresholds at low concentrations.
source: Indeed, it has been demonstrated that Zld can extend the effective range of the dorsal-ventral morphogen Dorsal and aid in establishing concentration thresholds and interpreting the gradient at low concentrations, while the requirement for Zld is less significant at high concentrations (Nien et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nien et al., 2011.

claim: Zld contributes to activation of target genes at low concentrations of Bcd protein.
source: Previous work has also suggested that Zld contributes to activation of target genes at low concentrations of Bcd protein (Xu et al., 2014), and a recent study demonstrated optically that in the absence of Zld, Bcd occupancy on chromatin in the posterior of the embryo is reduced (Mir et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2014 and Mir et al., 2017.

claim: In the absence of Zld, Bcd occupancy on chromatin in the posterior of the embryo is reduced.
source: Previous work has also suggested that Zld contributes to activation of target genes at low concentrations of Bcd protein (Xu et al., 2014), and a recent study demonstrated optically that in the absence of Zld, Bcd occupancy on chromatin in the posterior of the embryo is reduced (Mir et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mir et al., 2017.

claim: Transforming a concentration-sensitive Bcd target enhancer into a Zld dependent enhancer would increase the accessibility and therefore the sensitivity of that region in vivo.
source: These studies, in combination with the work presented here, allow us to predict that transforming a concentration-sensitive Bcd target enhancer into a Zld dependent enhancer would increase the accessibility and therefore the sensitivity of that region in vivo.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the combined data and previous studies.

claim: Adding increasing numbers of Zld sites to an inactive Bcd-bound enhancer can drive increasingly posterior gene expression.
source: Indeed, Xu, et al. have previously demonstrated that adding increasing numbers of Zld sites to an inactive Bcd-bound enhancer can drive increasingly posterior gene expression (Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2014.

claim: The increase in gene expression from the HC_45 reporter observed by Xu et al. is the result of increasing the accessibility of the enhancer region.
source: We posit that the increase in gene expression from this reporter observed in their work is the result of increasing the accessibility of the enhancer region.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the authors' model.

claim: At high concentrations, Bcd's activity is similar to Zld.
source: Interestingly, adding four additional Bcd sites to this reporter also activates anterior gene expression. This suggests that at high concentrations, Bcd's activity is similar to Zld.
evidence: This is inferred from the reporter expression data.

claim: Without Zld to keep the caudal enhancer open in posterior nuclei, activation of the reporter gene becomes entirely dependent on Bcd.
source: Alternately, when we replace Zld sites with Bcd sites in an enhancer that drives posterior expression, the expression domain shifts to the anterior of the embryo. This demonstrates that without Zld to keep the enhancer open in posterior nuclei, activation of the reporter gene becomes entirely dependent on Bcd, effectively shifting this reporter from a concentration-insensitive to concentration-sensitive enhancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the reporter expression data.

claim: Zld contributes to the accessibility of Bcd target genes throughout the embryo, while high levels of Bcd can drive accessibility independently and activate gene expression at a subset of targets in the anterior of the embryo.
source: This finding fits with both previously reported findings and the model proposed in our study. Namely, that Zld contributes to the accessibility of Bcd target genes throughout the embryo, while high levels of Bcd can drive accessibility independently and activate gene expression at a subset of targets in the anterior of the embryo.
evidence: This is a summary of the model inferred from the combined data.

claim: The C-terminus of Bcd is required for interactions with components of the Sin3A/HDAC repressor complex.
source: Previous work has shown that various domains of the Bcd protein are required for interactions with both co-activators and co-repressors. The N-terminus of Bcd is required for interactions with components of the Sin3A/HDAC repressor complex, and these interactions are proposed to play a role in reducing Bcd's transcriptional activation activity (Zhao et al., 2003; Zhu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhao et al., 2003 and Zhu et al., 2001.

claim: Multiple Bcd domains, including the C-terminus, are required for interaction with CREB-binding protein (CBP), which has histone acetyltransferase activity.
source: Multiple Bcd domains, including the C-terminus, are required for interaction with CREB-binding protein (CBP), which has histone acetyltransferase activity (Fu and Ma, 2005; Fu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fu and Ma, 2005 and Fu et al., 2004.

claim: In the truncated Bcd construct, the interaction with CBP may be disrupted.
source: It is possible that in our truncated Bcd construct, this interaction with CBP is disrupted.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the truncation data.

claim: CBP is thought to play a role in increasing chromatin accessibility for transcription factors.
source: As CBP is thought to play a role in increasing chromatin accessibility for transcription factors (Chan and La Thangue, 2001), the loss of this interaction could lead to the reduced binding to sensitive targets that we observe in embryos with truncated Bcd.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chan and La Thangue, 2001.

claim: The loss of CBP interaction could lead to the reduced binding to sensitive targets observed in embryos with truncated Bcd.
source: As CBP is thought to play a role in increasing chromatin accessibility for transcription factors (Chan and La Thangue, 2001), the loss of this interaction could lead to the reduced binding to sensitive targets that we observe in embryos with truncated Bcd.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the truncation data and CBP function.

claim: Concentration-insensitive targets do not depend on Bcd to establish an open chromatin state.
source: The targets that we have classified as concentration-insensitive do not depend on Bcd to establish an open chromatin state.
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq data.

claim: Concentration-insensitive sites are opened by other chromatin remodeling factors, or are inherently more likely to be nucleosome-free based on their underlying sequence.
source: This suggests that these sites are opened by other chromatin remodeling factors, or are inherently more likely to be nucleosome-free based on their underlying sequence.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the ATAC-seq data.

claim: Transcription factors can compete with nucleosomes for access to their DNA binding sites.
source: It has previously been suggested that transcription factors can compete with nucleosomes for access to their DNA binding sites (Mirny, 2010; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mirny, 2010 and Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Cooperative binding of Bcd to nucleosome-associated enhancers would require a high concentration of Bcd protein.
source: This could occur through cooperative binding to nucleosome-associated enhancers: if one Bcd molecule could gain access to a binding site that was protected by a nucleosome, it could recruit additional Bcd protein molecules to bind to nearby sites and occlude nucleosome binding. This cooperativity would require a high concentration of Bcd protein, fitting with our observation that Bcd influences accessibility more strongly at high concentrations.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the model.

claim: Bcd cannot bind to its most sensitive targets without its C-terminal domains.
source: However, our experiments with a truncated Bcd protein reveal that Bcd cannot bind to its most sensitive targets without its C-terminal domains.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data with truncated Bcd.

claim: Many of the residues implicated in cooperative binding reside in the Bcd homeodomain.
source: As many of the residues that have been implicated in cooperative binding reside in the Bcd homeodomain (Burz and Hanes, 2001), we would expect this truncated Bcd to bind cooperatively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burz and Hanes, 2001.

claim: The truncated Bcd finding supports a model in which Bcd is actively remodeling chromatin, either directly or more likely by interacting with chromatin remodeling factors through its C-terminus.
source: This finding therefore supports a model in which Bcd is actively remodeling chromatin, either directly or more likely by interacting with chromatin remodeling factors through its C-terminus.
evidence: This is inferred from the truncated Bcd data.

claim: Bcd provides one of the first cues to break the symmetry of the embryonic body plan.
source: As a maternally supplied factor, Bcd provides one of the first cues to the break the symmetry of the embryonic body plan.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Bcd function.

claim: Symmetry breaking by Bcd occurs first at the level of chromatin accessibility, as Bcd drives the opening of its most concentration-sensitive target enhancers in anterior nuclei.
source: Our results suggest that this symmetry breaking occurs first at the level of chromatin accessibility, as Bcd drives the opening of its most concentration-sensitive target enhancers in anterior nuclei.
evidence: This is inferred from the ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data.

claim: Zld is proposed to act as a pioneer factor at early embryonic enhancers with a high intrinsic nucleosome barrier.
source: Another maternal factor, Zld, is proposed to act as a pioneer factor at early embryonic enhancers with a high intrinsic nucleosome barrier. By binding to these enhancers, Zld depletes them of nucleosomes and allows patterning transcription factors to bind and activate gene expression (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2015.

claim: Bcd influences the accessibility primarily of its concentration-sensitive targets, which also exhibit a high predicted nucleosome barrier.
source: We have demonstrated here that Bcd influences the accessibility primarily of its concentration-sensitive targets, which also exhibit a high predicted nucleosome barrier (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by ATAC-seq and nucleosome prediction data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Bcd may be exhibiting pioneer-like activity at high concentrations, driving accessibility of concentration-sensitive sites prior to transcriptional activation.
source: This raises the possibility that Bcd may be exhibiting pioneer-like activity at high concentrations, driving accessibility of these sites prior to transcriptional activation.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the data.

claim: It is unlikely that Bcd is unique in its ability to influence the local chromatin accessibility of its targets.
source: It is unlikely that Bcd is unique in its ability to influence the local chromatin accessibility of its targets.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning.

claim: The homeodomain transcription factor Cdx2 influences the chromatin accessibility of its targets during posterior axial elongation in mouse embryos.
source: Recent work in mouse embryos has shown that another homeodomain transcription factor, Cdx2, influences the chromatin accessibility of its targets during posterior axial elongation (Amin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Amin et al., 2016.

claim: It will be of interest to assess whether other developmental transcription factors can drive accessibility of their genomic targets while the chromatin state of the genome is being remodeled during early development.
source: It will therefore be of interest to assess whether other developmental transcription factors can drive accessibility of their genomic targets while the chromatin state of the genome is being remodeled during early development.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about future research directions.
